entries.clue: Like something flapping – say, insect going round (8)

indicatorNotes.going round: Something that goes round another thing closes about it, so the insect's letters end up on both sides of the other word.

blocks.note: the commonest three-letter insect in the language
to say something is to utter it

annotation.surface: An insect circling something that flaps in the wind.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the trap: it usually flags a homophone, and here it is simply the verb, to utter. FLUTTERY takes the -y ending that turns a noun into 'like a flutter', which is why the definition begins 'Like'.
annotation.definitionFit: Fluttery describes anything that flaps in short quick movements — a curtain at an open window, or a nervous heartbeat.

entries.clue: Disciple upset before he had had some loaves and fishes? (6)

indicatorNotes.upset: Something upset has been turned over, and in a down entry that means its letters are read back up the column.
indicatorNotes.before: What comes before something else is reached first, so these letters take the top of the column.

blocks.note: a son is a follower taught by a master — the word a teacher uses for the young man he instructs
'he had' contracts to he'd

annotation.surface: A disciple in a huff before he had eaten his share of the miracle picnic.
annotation.walkthrough: Nosh came into British English from Yiddish and means food, so to nosh is to eat. The clue's two 'had's sit side by side: the first belongs to the wordplay, the second opens the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To nosh is to eat, so whoever was fed at the miracle of the loaves and fishes noshed.

entries.clue: Sore member of the family hiding under something warm (8)

indicatorNotes.hiding under: To hide under something is to take cover beneath it, and beneath in a down entry means further down the column.

blocks.note: what keeps an animal warm, and the coat made out of it
your mother's or father's brother

annotation.surface: A sore relative hiding underneath something warm.
annotation.walkthrough: A furuncle is the medical name for a boil, which is why 'Sore' is a noun here rather than the adjective the sentence offers. Doctors still write it on notes; patients never say it.
annotation.definitionFit: A furuncle is a boil — a red swelling coming up under the skin — and a sore in the noun sense is exactly that.

entries.clue: Jazz fan turned up with old mum in American city (6)

indicatorNotes.turned up: Turned up means lifted end over end, and in a down entry that reads the letters back up the column.

blocks.note: a cat is a jazz enthusiast, in the music's own slang
standard abbreviation
ma is the informal word for mother

annotation.surface: A jazz lover arriving with his elderly mother.
annotation.walkthrough: Tacoma sits on Puget Sound in Washington State, a little south of Seattle. 'Cat' for a jazz fan is the music's own 1940s slang, the same one that gave us hepcat.
annotation.definitionFit: Tacoma is a port city in Washington State, so 'American city' names it by example rather than by synonym.

entries.clue: Crude guy also accompanying prisoner on return (6)

indicatorNotes.on return: On return means coming back the way it went, and in an across entry the letters come back from right to left.

blocks.note: also = too
an old lag is a convict, a word left over from the days of transportation

annotation.surface: A rough sort of man keeping a convict company on the way back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lag' for a convict is still current in Britain in the phrase old lag, someone who has served several sentences. Galoot arrived here from American slang, where it began as sailors' talk for a raw recruit.
annotation.definitionFit: A galoot is a big clumsy oaf, which is the sort of man 'crude guy' describes.

entries.clue: Intelligent leader – kind inside (6)

indicatorNotes.inside: Something inside a phrase is already sitting among its letters, so nothing has to be built — only spotted.

blocks.note: six consecutive letters, starting partway through the first word and running into the second

annotation.surface: A clever boss who is kind underneath it all.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Leader' is the trap. It nearly always asks for a first letter, and here it is only more of the phrase the answer is buried in. The dash marks where the wordplay stops.
annotation.definitionFit: Gentle and kind are near synonyms for a manner: someone gentle deals with others mildly and considerately.

entries.clue: Greek character with blemish, not one monstrous type? (6)

indicatorNotes.not one: 'Not' takes something away and 'one' names what goes — the Roman numeral I, dropped from the letters just given.

blocks.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
a TAINT is a blemish, and it loses the I that stands for one

annotation.surface: A Greek character carrying a blemish, painted as something monstrous.
annotation.walkthrough: Greek letters are a setter's staple — mu, pi, eta, chi — and 'character' is the word that usually announces one. The question mark admits that a mutant is monstrous only in the films.
annotation.definitionFit: A mutant is a creature thrown up by a change in its genes, which is what makes it the monstrous type of science fiction.

entries.clue: Union less troubled or fighting? (6)

indicatorNotes.troubled: Something troubled has been stirred up and will not settle, so the letters it describes do not stay in the order they were printed.

blocks.note: TU is the British abbreviation for a trade union
the four letters of LESS, disarranged

annotation.surface: A trade union having a quieter time of it than usual.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark is a warning about grammar: 'fighting' has to be read as the noun, the thing that breaks out, rather than as what the union is doing. TU for a trade union is standard.
annotation.definitionFit: A tussle is a scuffle, a rough grappling struggle — fighting in its noun sense, one bout of it rather than the activity at large.

entries.clue: Requirement to do well in heat? This climate is awful (11)

annotation.definition: Requirement to do well in heat?

indicatorNotes.is awful: Calling the climate awful says it is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state have fallen out of their proper order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: A grumble that the weather here is dreadful for getting anything done.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heat' is the hinge: it belongs to the weather in the surface and to the running track in the definition, where a heat is a qualifying race. Eleven letters of fodder sit in plain sight beside it.
annotation.definitionFit: Athleticism is physical fitness and prowess — what a runner needs to get through a heat and into the final.

entries.clue: Steal money going round in school (6)

indicatorNotes.going round: Money that goes round comes back on itself, so these letters are read the other way about.
indicatorNotes.in: 'In' buries one piece inside another, so what comes before it goes within what comes after.

blocks.note: sch. is the abbreviation on a timetable or a street sign
tin is old slang for cash

annotation.surface: Cash doing the rounds of a school playground.
annotation.walkthrough: To snitch is to pinch as well as to tell tales, and it is the pinching sense the definition wants. 'Tin' for money is Victorian slang that now survives mostly in crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: To snitch something is to steal it — the petty-thieving sense, quite separate from the informer who snitches on you.

entries.clue: ‘Ladies and Gentlemen’ perhaps heard in French city (8)

indicatorNotes.heard: Heard means taken in by ear alone, so what counts is the noise the quoted words make, not how they are spelt.

blocks.note: the doors marked Ladies and Gentlemen are a pair of lavatories, and loo is the everyday British word for one

annotation.surface: A master of ceremonies opening his address somewhere in France.
annotation.walkthrough: The quoted words pretend to be the start of a speech; they are the signs on two doors. 'Perhaps' is there because they are only one example of how a pair of lavatories gets labelled.
annotation.definitionFit: Toulouse is the pink-brick city on the Garonne in south-west France, so 'French city' names it by example.

entries.clue: Sad saint may be found in Derbyshire cave (4,4)

blocks.note: to feel blue is to feel low
St John the Evangelist, reduced to his first name as saints usually are here

annotation.surface: A gloomy saint turning up down a cave in Derbyshire.
annotation.walkthrough: The stone is a purple-and-yellow fluorspar mined at Castleton in the Peak District and nowhere else on earth; its name comes from the French bleu-jaune, blue-yellow. The cavern was named after what came out of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Blue John names both the banded fluorspar and the Castleton cavern it is dug from, a show cave open to visitors in Derbyshire.

entries.clue: Delicious cold food served after sign to remove something (10)

indicatorNotes.after: What comes after something else is reached later, so the cold food takes the back of the answer and the sign goes in front of it.

blocks.note: dele is the proofreader's mark ordering a letter to be struck out
standard abbreviation, as on a tap
a house that keeps a good table sets out good food

annotation.surface: Cold food arriving once somebody has signalled for something to be taken away.
annotation.walkthrough: Dele is printer's Latin for delete, still pencilled into margins, and 'table' for food is the sense in 'keeps a good table'. Neither belongs to the surface's world of dinner and hand signals.
annotation.definitionFit: Delectable means delightful to taste, the word a menu reaches for when delicious has started to sound plain.

entries.clue: I tap my chest, animatedly commiserating (11)

indicatorNotes.animatedly: Doing something animatedly means doing it with everything in motion, and letters in motion do not stay where they were put.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters

annotation.surface: Somebody thumping their own chest while offering condolences.
annotation.walkthrough: Beating the breast is the old gesture of grief, so the fodder acts out the definition it hides. The comma is the only sign that the first four words are raw material rather than description.
annotation.definitionFit: To be sympathetic is to feel with someone in their trouble, which is what commiserating with them amounts to.

entries.clue: I spit egg out, being most disgusting at the meal? (8)

indicatorNotes.out: Spitting something out sends it anywhere but where it was, and letters sent out like that land in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Somebody spitting out their egg and disgracing themselves at dinner.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue describes its own answer: the person spitting the egg out is the one behaving worst at table. 'Out' hides its instruction inside the phrasal verb 'spit out', where it reads as part of the action.
annotation.definitionFit: Piggiest is the superlative of piggy — behaving most like a pig, which at a meal means greedy and revolting.

entries.clue: Damages home fitting panels below (8)

indicatorNotes.fitting: To fit a part is to set it where it belongs, which is the instruction to join these pieces up.
indicatorNotes.below: Below in a down entry means further down the column, so the panels take the bottom of the answer.

blocks.note: someone who is in is at home
a jury is a panel of twelve, and the clue wants more than one

annotation.surface: Damage done at home while panels are fitted along the bottom of a wall.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Damages' is the plural noun, not the verb the sentence offers — and in its legal sense damages are what a panel of twelve awards, which is where the second piece comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Injuries and damages both name harms suffered, in the plural noun sense an insurance claim uses rather than the verb to damage.

entries.clue: Got to the top – said to be so offended (6)

indicatorNotes.said to be so: Saying a word is not spelling it, and this asks for one that matches only out loud.

blocks.note: to reach the summit is to have peaked, and the two spellings are said exactly the same way

annotation.surface: Somebody reported to have got to the top and taken offence.
annotation.walkthrough: Piqued comes from the French pique, a prick or a sting, so to be piqued is to be stung in your pride. Nothing but the sound connects it to a summit.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone piqued has had their pride nettled — offended in the mild, sulky sense rather than outraged.

entries.clue: Top of country house that’s horrible for bird (6)

indicatorNotes.Top of: The top of a word in a down entry is the letter it starts with, and that single letter is all this asks for.

blocks.note: the first letter of COUNTRY
ho. is the standard abbreviation on an address
ugh is the noise of disgust

annotation.surface: A country house so horrible it has been left to the birds.
annotation.walkthrough: A chough is a black crow with a curved red bill and red legs, nesting on sea cliffs and long a Cornish emblem. The word rhymes with rough, which is no help at all in spelling it.
annotation.definitionFit: The chough is a member of the crow family, so 'bird' is the broad class the answer belongs to.

entries.clue: Minister transporting a gent around in old vehicle (7,3)

indicatorNotes.transporting: A minister transporting somebody is carrying them along inside, so one piece rides within the other.
indicatorNotes.around: A gent moved around has been shifted from where he was standing, and letters shifted about come out in a new order.

blocks.note: a vicar is the minister of a Church of England parish
the five letters of A GENT, shifted out of order

annotation.surface: A vicar giving a gentleman a lift in his old motor.
annotation.walkthrough: Ministers in crosswords are vicars, parsons or MPs, and this one is the parish sort. He and the car belong to the same English village daydream, which is why no word of the sentence feels out of place.
annotation.definitionFit: A vintage car is one built between 1919 and 1930, the collectors' bracket — an old vehicle in the most specific sense.

entries.clue: Be a swinger at the club, stripped to the waist? (3,3)

annotation.definition: Be a swinger at the club

blocks.clueFragment: Be a swinger at the club
blocks.note: the opening drive of a golf hole, struck from a little peg with a full swing
clothing rather than golf: the man has taken off the shirt that is named after a letter of the alphabet

annotation.surface: A party animal at the nightclub dancing with his shirt off.
annotation.walkthrough: The club changes hands between the two halves — a golf club in the first, a nightclub in the picture the sentence paints. The shirt is the one named for the letter its shape makes.
annotation.definitionFit: To tee off is to play the first shot of a hole; and a man stripped to the waist has his tee, his T-shirt, off.

entries.clue: Musician and artist married overlooking water abroad (6)

indicatorNotes.overlooking: To overlook something is to stand above it, so in a down entry what overlooks takes the higher squares of the column.

blocks.note: RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's standard artist
standard abbreviation, as on a form
eau is the French for water

annotation.surface: A musician and an artist marrying in sight of the sea abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Overlooking' is the trap: it usually means failing to notice, which would take letters away, and here it only means standing above. Jean-Philippe Rameau wrote French baroque opera and the theory book that taught Europe about chords.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Musician' is a definition by example: Jean-Philippe Rameau was the leading French composer of the eighteenth century's first half.

entries.clue: See 11
See 23
What disturbs us – a mercurial US ‘emperor’ (6,8)

indicatorNotes.disturbs: Disturbing something leaves it unsettled and out of place, and letters left out of place have to be put back in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, fourteen letters, with the two-letter word counted at each end

annotation.surface: Some volatile American figure who unsettles everybody and gets called an emperor.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the giveaway that no American is meant: the United States has no emperors, and the one wanted here ruled Rome and wrote the Meditations. 'Mercurial' is the opposite of what a Stoic was famous for.
annotation.definitionFit: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180, the last of the emperors remembered as good ones — the quotation marks are the surface's doing.

entries.clue: Brill employment brings ease (6)

blocks.note: both are slang for excellent — brill short for brilliant, def out of hip-hop
the use of a thing is its employment

annotation.surface: A brilliant job of work that makes life easier.
annotation.walkthrough: Both slang words date themselves: brill is 1980s British playground, def is 1980s hip-hop. The definition is a verb borrowed from bomb disposal — what you do to a row or a crisis rather than to a bomb.
annotation.definitionFit: To defuse a situation is to take the danger out of it, which is to ease the tension in it.

entries.clue: He sang about an Indian god (6)

indicatorNotes.about: About means round and round, so the letters it touches are turned out of the order they arrived in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A man singing on the subject of a Hindu deity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like the preposition that follows 'sang' and is the shuffle instruction instead. Ganesh, the elephant-headed son of Shiva, is the remover of obstacles, invoked at the start of anything new.
annotation.definitionFit: Ganesh is one of the most worshipped gods of Hinduism, so 'an Indian god' names him by example.
